This report contains my prompts, code, results and discussion together. The R code and its figures appear in the sections below. The cross-validation loops can take a few minutes to finish.

## Data

Wolfcamp contains 85 piezometric-head measurements from an aquifer in Texas. The geoR documentation gives coordinates in km and heads in metres. These are continuous measurements at spatial locations, not longitude and latitude. I use ordinary Euclidean distances in these coordinates. Reference in R: help("wolfcamp", package = "geoR").

# Part 1: How the prompt changes the analysis

**Bad prompt**

> "Confirm that the Wolfcamp data are spatially dependent. Use R to draw a variogram and give me a yes-or-no answer."

**Good prompt**

> "Using wolfcamp from the geoR package in R, assess whether there is evidence of spatial structure in the measured piezometric heads. First inspect the data structure, sample size, missing values, duplicate locations, and coordinate/measurement units. Identify the spatial data type and justify an appropriate diagnostic rather than applying a list of methods automatically. Provide runnable R code, a map, and an empirical semivariogram with explicit distance bins and pair counts. Explain what patterns would and would not support spatial dependence. If you use a statistical comparison, state its null hypothesis and assumptions, and set a seed for reproducibility. Check whether a broad change in the mean across space could affect the raw-data interpretation; flag this limitation without requiring a full trend model. Report only numerical results actually calculated and conclude cautiously, distinguishing raw spatial structure from residual dependence."

```{r load-data}
required_packages <- c("geoR", "gstat", "MBA", "sp")
missing_packages <- required_packages[
  !vapply(required_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  stop("Please install these packages first: ",
       paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "))
}
data("wolfcamp", package = "geoR")
out <- "homework1_results"
dir.create(out, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## 1A. My analysis for the bad prompt

The calculation is valid; the prompt's framing and requested conclusion are weak. A variogram by itself does not justify a definitive yes/no.

```{r raw-variogram, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
v_bad <- geoR::variog(wolfcamp, messages = FALSE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
plot(v_bad, pch = 19, xlab = "Distance (km)",
     ylab = expression("Semivariance (" * m^2 * ")"),
     main = "Minimal analysis: raw Wolfcamp semivariogram")
```

## 1B. My analysis for the good prompt

Source for units and description: help("wolfcamp", package = "geoR"). These are continuous point-referenced measurements at fixed locations. Coordinates are in km; piezometric heads are in metres.

```{r data-checks}
dat <- data.frame(x = wolfcamp$coords[, 1],
                  y = wolfcamp$coords[, 2], head = wolfcamp$data)
checks <- data.frame(
  observations = nrow(dat),
  missing_values = sum(is.na(dat)),
  duplicate_locations = sum(duplicated(dat[c("x", "y")]))
)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(dat))),
          checks$duplicate_locations == 0)
write.csv(checks, file.path(out, "data_checks.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(dat, file.path(out, "wolfcamp_data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r explore-data, fig.width=10, fig.height=7, fig.keep="last"}
# Explore the spatial arrangement, distribution and possible mean trend.
quartile <- cut(dat$head, quantile(dat$head, seq(0, 1, 0.25)),
                include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)
palette <- c("#2166AC", "#67A9CF", "#FDAE61", "#B2182B")
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1))
plot(dat$x, dat$y, asp = 1, pch = 19, col = palette[quartile],
     xlab = "X coordinate (km)", ylab = "Y coordinate (km)",
     main = "Locations coloured by head quartile")
legend("topright", legend = c("Q1: lowest", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4: highest"),
       col = palette, pch = 19, cex = 0.75, bty = "n")
hist(dat$head, breaks = "FD", col = "#D9EAF1", border = "white",
     xlab = "Piezometric head (m)", main = "Head distribution")
plot(dat$x, dat$head, pch = 19, col = "#365A73",
     xlab = "X coordinate (km)", ylab = "Head (m)", main = "Head versus X")
lines(lowess(dat$x, dat$head), col = "#B2182B", lwd = 2)
plot(dat$y, dat$head, pch = 19, col = "#365A73",
     xlab = "Y coordinate (km)", ylab = "Head (m)", main = "Head versus Y")
lines(lowess(dat$y, dat$head), col = "#B2182B", lwd = 2)
```

```{r variogram-bins}
# Explicit bins: 12 equal-width intervals up to half the maximum distance.
# Longer lags are omitted here because they are less local and can be
# sensitive to the sampling geometry. This is a diagnostic choice.
distance_matrix <- as.matrix(dist(dat[c("x", "y")]))
pairs <- which(lower.tri(distance_matrix), arr.ind = TRUE)
distance <- distance_matrix[pairs]
max_lag <- max(distance) / 2
v_good <- geoR::variog(wolfcamp,
                      breaks = seq(0, max_lag, length.out = 13),
                      max.dist = max_lag, messages = FALSE)
variogram_table <- data.frame(lag_km = v_good$u,
                             semivariance_m2 = v_good$v,
                             pairs = v_good$n)
write.csv(variogram_table, file.path(out, "variogram_bins.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r permutation-comparison}
# Transparent permutation comparison for RAW spatial structure.
# H0: measured heads are exchangeable across the fixed locations.
# Statistic: mean semivariance among the closest 10% of all site pairs.
# This neighbourhood is defined by coordinates alone, before examining
# head differences. Small values indicate unusually similar neighbours.
near_cutoff <- unname(quantile(distance, 0.10))
near <- pairs[distance <= near_cutoff, , drop = FALSE]
near_semivariance <- function(z) {
  mean((z[near[, 1]] - z[near[, 2]])^2) / 2
}
observed <- near_semivariance(dat$head)
RNGkind("Mersenne-Twister", "Inversion", "Rejection")
set.seed(2026)
B <- 9999
null_statistics <- replicate(B, near_semivariance(sample(dat$head)))
p_value <- (1 + sum(null_statistics <= observed)) / (B + 1)

results <- data.frame(
  n = nrow(dat), total_pairs = nrow(pairs),
  maximum_distance_km = max(distance), variogram_max_lag_km = max_lag,
  near_cutoff_km = near_cutoff, near_pairs = nrow(near),
  observed_near_semivariance_m2 = observed,
  permutation_mean_m2 = mean(null_statistics),
  sample_variance_m2 = var(dat$head),
  observed_to_permutation_mean = observed / mean(null_statistics),
  permutations = B, permutation_p_value = p_value
)
write.csv(results, file.path(out, "numerical_results.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(null_semivariance_m2 = null_statistics),
          file.path(out, "permutation_statistics.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r spatial-diagnostics, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.5, fig.keep="last"}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(v_good, pch = 19, xlab = "Distance (km)",
     ylab = expression("Semivariance (" * m^2 * ")"),
     main = "Raw semivariogram: explicit bins",
     ylim = c(0, max(v_good$v) * 1.13))
text(v_good$u, v_good$v, labels = v_good$n, pos = 3, cex = 0.65)
mtext("Numbers above points are pair counts", side = 3, cex = 0.7)
hist(null_statistics, breaks = 35, col = "#D9EAF1", border = "white",
     xlim = range(c(observed, null_statistics)),
     xlab = expression("Nearby-pair semivariance (" * m^2 * ")"),
     main = "Randomly shuffled heads")
abline(v = observed, col = "#B2182B", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = sprintf("Observed = %.1f; p = %.4f", observed, p_value),
       col = "#B2182B", lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

```{r part1-numeric-output, results="hide"}
print(checks)
print(round(results, 6))
print(transform(variogram_table,
                lag_km = round(lag_km, 2),
                semivariance_m2 = round(semivariance_m2, 2)))
cat("\nInterpretation: assess raw spatial structure using the plots and\n",
    "permutation comparison together. A changing spatial mean violates\n",
    "exchangeability too, so this is NOT a test of residual dependence.\n",
    "No trend model has been fitted or removed in this exercise.\n")
```

## 1C. My results and discussion

I found 85 observations, with no missing values or duplicate locations. Both variograms rise with distance. In the explicit-bin variogram, semivariance increases from 1,563.74 m^2 in the first bin (centre 9.09 km) to 36,953.13 m^2 in the last bin (centre 209.02 km). Semivariance is half the average squared difference between the measurements in a distance bin. A rising pattern means that nearby measurements tend to be more similar. A flat pattern would offer less evidence of this relationship, but would not prove independence. Bin centres are not estimates of a correlation range.

For the closest 10% of pairs, the distance cutoff is 53.92 km. These 357 pairs have mean semivariance 2,429.51 m^2, compared with 34,724.07 m^2 after shuffling. My observed value is about 7% of the shuffled mean. None of the 9,999 permutations gave a value this small, so the corrected Monte Carlo p-value is 0.0001. This is the smallest possible value with this simulation, not a zero probability. I shuffled whole sets of heads, rather than treating overlapping pairs as independent observations.

My bad prompt already suggests the answer by saying "confirm". Although its variogram is useful, the prompt encourages me to jump to a yes/no conclusion. My good prompt makes me check the data, explain my choices, and show how someone else can reproduce the result. The variograms use different bins and distance limits, so their individual values should not be compared as though the settings were identical.

The map shows higher heads towards the southwest and lower heads towards the northeast. This broad trend can also produce the increasing variogram and the small permutation p-value. The shuffling comparison assumes that heads can be exchanged between locations under its null hypothesis; a changing mean also breaks that assumption. Pooling all directions into one variogram may also hide differences between directions.

I conclude that the RAW data show strong spatial structure. I have not shown that dependence remains after removing the broad trend. The good prompt improves how I check and interpret the result; its advantage is not simply that it produces a longer answer.

## 1D. Recorded AI responses and critical comparison

### How these responses were recorded

I added this section after receiving the professor's feedback. The two responses below were generated directly by ChatGPT/Codex on 19 October 2026, using the exact prompts already shown in Part 1. They are new responses for this revision, rather than a recovered transcript of the original preparation of the homework. Each response is reproduced in full between its start and end markers.

Both responses were produced in the same ongoing conversation. The AI already had access to the report, its numerical results and the professor's feedback. Therefore, this is a documented comparison of these two responses, not an independent experiment showing that the prompt alone caused the differences. The original analyses in Sections 1A–1C remain the worked analyses of the two prompts.

The R code in the response blocks is displayed with `eval=FALSE` to keep the AI record separate from the existing calculations when knitting the report. Both response code blocks were checked separately in R by the AI assistant. The student-style evaluations below were also drafted with AI assistance; they are presented separately from the AI responses being evaluated.

### Exact bad prompt

> "Confirm that the Wolfcamp data are spatially dependent. Use R to draw a variogram and give me a yes-or-no answer."

### AI response to the bad prompt

**Start of AI response — ChatGPT/Codex**

Yes, the raw Wolfcamp measurements show evidence of spatial structure: the empirical semivariogram increases with distance, meaning that nearby measurements tend to be more similar than measurements farther apart.

```{r ai-bad-response-code, eval=FALSE}
# Install geoR first if needed: install.packages("geoR")
data("wolfcamp", package = "geoR")
v <- geoR::variog(wolfcamp, messages = FALSE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
plot(v, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Semivariance (m^2)",
     main = "Raw Wolfcamp semivariogram")
```

This gives a graphical indication, not a formal significance test. A broad spatial trend can also produce an increasing raw semivariogram, so this result does not establish that spatial dependence remains after removing that trend.

**End of AI response**

### My evaluation of the bad-prompt response

The response gives a reasonable first description of the data. A semivariogram is appropriate for continuous measurements at spatial locations, and the explanation of increasing semivariance is correct: larger distances tend to correspond to larger squared differences. The code ran successfully in the separate R check and produced the raw variogram.

The answer is more cautious than the wording of my prompt. It explicitly mentions trend and says that the graph is not a significance test. Therefore, I should not describe this particular AI response as ignoring trend or proving residual dependence. It did neither of those things. The opening "Yes" is still easy to read too strongly, so I would retain the narrower wording "evidence of spatial structure in the raw measurements."

Its main weakness is the lack of supporting checks. It does not inspect missing values or duplicate locations, explain the default distance bins, report pair counts, or discuss the assumptions needed to interpret a pooled variogram as a description of a stationary spatial process. The code is runnable, but the reader receives little guidance on assessing its sensitivity to these choices. It gives no numerical p-value or fitted range, so there is no unsupported numerical claim to correct.

### Exact good prompt

> "Using wolfcamp from the geoR package in R, assess whether there is evidence of spatial structure in the measured piezometric heads. First inspect the data structure, sample size, missing values, duplicate locations, and coordinate/measurement units. Identify the spatial data type and justify an appropriate diagnostic rather than applying a list of methods automatically. Provide runnable R code, a map, and an empirical semivariogram with explicit distance bins and pair counts. Explain what patterns would and would not support spatial dependence. If you use a statistical comparison, state its null hypothesis and assumptions, and set a seed for reproducibility. Check whether a broad change in the mean across space could affect the raw-data interpretation; flag this limitation without requiring a full trend model. Report only numerical results actually calculated and conclude cautiously, distinguishing raw spatial structure from residual dependence."

### AI response to the good prompt

**Start of AI response — ChatGPT/Codex**

I would use an empirical semivariogram because Wolfcamp contains continuous piezometric-head measurements at spatial locations. The `geoR` documentation gives coordinates in kilometres and heads in metres. These coordinates should be treated as Cartesian coordinates, not longitude and latitude. The data have 85 observations, with no missing values or duplicate locations.

I first inspect the measurements and their spatial arrangement. Then I use 12 equal-width distance bins up to half the maximum pair distance and report how many pairs contribute to each bin. This distance limit is a diagnostic choice, not an estimated correlation range.

For an additional comparison, I calculate the mean semivariance of the closest 10% of location pairs and compare it with randomly shuffled heads. Under the null hypothesis, heads are exchangeable across the fixed locations: reassigning the observed heads to those locations should not systematically change the statistic. Small observed values indicate that nearby measurements are unusually similar under this null.

```{r ai-good-response-code, eval=FALSE}
# Install geoR first if needed: install.packages("geoR")
data("wolfcamp", package = "geoR")
str(wolfcamp)
# Units and data description: help("wolfcamp", package = "geoR")
d <- data.frame(x = wolfcamp$coords[, 1],
                y = wolfcamp$coords[, 2], head = wolfcamp$data)
checks_ai <- data.frame(
  observations = nrow(d),
  missing_values = sum(is.na(d)),
  duplicate_locations = sum(duplicated(d[c("x", "y")]))
)
print(checks_ai)
print(summary(d))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(d))),
          checks_ai$duplicate_locations == 0)

# Map and simple checks for a broad change in head across space.
group <- cut(d$head, quantile(d$head, seq(0, 1, 0.25)),
             include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)
colours <- c("#2166AC", "#67A9CF", "#FDAE61", "#B2182B")
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(d$x, d$y, asp = 1, pch = 19, col = colours[group],
     xlab = "X (km)", ylab = "Y (km)", main = "Wolfcamp locations")
legend("topright", c("Lowest", "Q2", "Q3", "Highest"),
       pch = 19, col = colours, cex = 0.65, bty = "n")
hist(d$head, xlab = "Head (m)", main = "Head distribution")
plot(d$x, d$head, xlab = "X (km)", ylab = "Head (m)")
lines(lowess(d$x, d$head), col = "red")
plot(d$y, d$head, xlab = "Y (km)", ylab = "Head (m)")
lines(lowess(d$y, d$head), col = "red")

# Empirical semivariogram with explicit distance bins and pair counts.
D <- as.matrix(dist(d[c("x", "y")]))
ij <- which(lower.tri(D), arr.ind = TRUE)
distances <- D[ij]
limit <- max(distances) / 2
v <- geoR::variog(wolfcamp, max.dist = limit,
                  breaks = seq(0, limit, length.out = 13),
                  messages = FALSE)
print(data.frame(bin_centre_km = v$u, semivariance_m2 = v$v,
                 pairs = v$n))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
plot(v, pch = 19, xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Semivariance (m^2)",
     ylim = c(0, max(v$v) * 1.15))
text(v$u, v$v, labels = v$n, pos = 3, cex = 0.7)

# Nearby pairs are selected using coordinates alone.
cutoff <- unname(quantile(distances, 0.10))
near <- ij[distances <= cutoff, , drop = FALSE]
near_semivariance <- function(z) {
  mean((z[near[, 1]] - z[near[, 2]])^2) / 2
}
observed <- near_semivariance(d$head)
RNGkind("Mersenne-Twister", "Inversion", "Rejection")
set.seed(2026)
B <- 9999
shuffled <- replicate(B, near_semivariance(sample(d$head)))
p_value <- (1 + sum(shuffled <= observed)) / (B + 1)
print(c(cutoff_km = cutoff, nearby_pairs = nrow(near),
        observed_semivariance_m2 = observed,
        shuffled_mean_m2 = mean(shuffled), p_value = p_value))
```

The numerical results already calculated in this analysis are: the distance limit is 218.10 km; nearby pairs are at most 53.92 km apart; and their observed mean semivariance is 2,429.51 m², compared with a shuffled mean of 34,724.07 m². There are 357 nearby pairs. The one-sided Monte Carlo p-value is 0.0001, the minimum attainable with 9,999 permutations and this correction. It should not be reported as zero.

The increasing semivariogram supports a distance-related pattern in the raw measurements. A roughly flat semivariogram would offer less evidence of such a pattern at the distances examined, although it would not prove independence. Pair counts help assess how much information supports each bin; the pairs are not independent because they can share observations.

There are two important limits to the interpretation. First, the map and coordinate plots show a broad spatial change in head. A changing mean contributes to the raw squared differences, so the raw semivariogram cannot isolate residual dependence. Interpreting it as a single stationary variogram would require assumptions about the mean and the dependence structure; pooling directions also assumes that an average across directions is informative. Second, the permutation null is stronger than simply assuming independent observations with possibly different means. A changing spatial mean can also cause rejection of exchangeability. The code shuffles entire vectors of heads, not individual pair differences.

My conclusion is that the raw Wolfcamp measurements show strong spatial structure. These calculations do not establish dependence remaining after trend removal. A later analysis would need to model the broad trend and examine the residuals before making that more specific claim.

**End of AI response**

### My evaluation of the good-prompt response

This answer is easier to check because it identifies the data type and units, inspects the observations, and explains its choice of a semivariogram. Its code ran successfully in the separate R check. The bin counts and the numerical results agreed with the calculations already reported in Part 1. This supports those specific numerical claims; it does not mean that every statistical interpretation should be accepted automatically.

The variogram interpretation is correct. The answer explains both the increasing pattern observed here and what a flat pattern would mean. It also correctly separates a broad spatial trend from dependence that might remain after removing that trend. I therefore accept its conclusion about raw spatial structure, while keeping its limit on claims about residual dependence.

The explanation of the permutation comparison is especially useful. It states exchangeability across locations as the null hypothesis and explains why a changing mean can violate it. It does not treat the 357 nearby pairs as 357 independent observations. It also describes 0.0001 as a Monte Carlo p-value rather than an exact probability or proof of a stationary spatial model.

The response still leaves choices that deserve judgment. The 12 bins, the half-distance limit and the closest 10% of pairs are reasonable diagnostic settings, but they are not the only possible settings. Their sensitivity has not been investigated here. It also does not fit a trend model or test residual dependence, which is consistent with the limits of the prompt. I would not extend its conclusion beyond what it actually checked.

### Comparison of the actual responses

| Point I checked | Response to the bad prompt | Response to the good prompt |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Method and data type | Uses an appropriate semivariogram but gives little justification. | Identifies continuous point-referenced data and explains why a semivariogram is suitable. |
| R code | Runnable short code using default variogram settings. | Runnable code with data checks, a map, explicit bins, pair counts and a reproducible permutation comparison. |
| Variogram interpretation | Correctly links rising semivariance to larger differences at longer distances. | Gives the same interpretation and also explains why a flat variogram would not prove independence. |
| Trend and residual dependence | Explicitly mentions trend and does not claim to have tested residual dependence. | Develops the distinction and explains its consequences for both diagnostics. |
| Assumptions | Says the graph is not a significance test, but gives little further detail. | Explains exchangeability, the effect of a changing mean and the limits of pooling distances and directions. |
| Numerical claims | Gives no p-value or fitted range. | Gives numerical values that were checked against executed R calculations. |
| Conclusion | The initial "Yes" needs to be read together with the later qualification. | Directly limits the conclusion to raw spatial structure. |

The weak prompt did not produce a completely wrong answer. It even produced a useful warning about trend, which I should acknowledge. The advantage of the good-prompt response is that more of its reasoning and assumptions can be checked. The difference is therefore about the support for the conclusion, not just the length of the answer. Since these responses share the earlier conversation context, I cannot claim that a fresh AI session would always show the same difference.

# Part 2: IDW and multilevel B-splines

**My prompt for Part 2**

> "Using the same Wolfcamp data, write clear R code for my homework. Build a function that chooses the IDW power p using gstat::idw and cross-validation. Compare tuned IDW with multilevel B-splines using predictions at the same held-out locations and RMSE in metres. Keep parameter selection inside the training data, so the held-out heads do not influence the choice of p. Use five outer folds for the comparison and leave-one-out cross-validation within each training set to choose p. Keep the B-spline settings fixed and state them. Then use all observations to make a 20 x 20 grid from the coordinate ranges. Use gstat::idw for IDW, MBA::mba.points for validation, and MBA::mba.surf for the grid. Explain why fitting errors or differences between the two maps are not proper measures of prediction accuracy. Include readable plots, the results actually calculated, and a short discussion in ordinary student language."

### My approach

IDW is a weighted average, with weights proportional to distance^(-p). A larger p gives more weight to nearby observations. I keep all training observations as possible neighbours and choose p from 0.5 to 8 by 0.5. For B-splines I use n = 1, m = 1 and h = 8 (the package defaults). I set these choices before looking at the comparison scores.

I cannot calculate prediction errors at the new grid points because I do not know their true heads. Instead, I hide observed values, predict at those locations, and compare predictions with the values I hid. My main score is RMSE = sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2)). A smaller RMSE is better; its unit is metres. I also report MAE in metres and mean error (predicted minus observed), where zero indicates no average overprediction or underprediction on these held-out observations.

## 2A. A function to choose the IDW power p

```{r idw-function}
# This short helper uses gstat's IDW, rather than reimplementing its weights.
predict_idw <- function(train, new_locations, p) {
  gstat::idw(
    head ~ 1, locations = ~ x + y, data = train,
    newdata = new_locations, idp = p, nmax = Inf, debug.level = 0
  )$var1.pred
}

# For each candidate p, leave out one observation at a time and predict it
# from the others. Choose the p with the smallest leave-one-out RMSE.
# The returned table lets me inspect the whole curve, not just its minimum.
choose_idw_p <- function(data, p_values = seq(0.5, 8, by = 0.5)) {
  stopifnot(nrow(data) >= 3, all(is.finite(p_values)), all(p_values > 0))
  cv_rmse <- numeric(length(p_values))

  for (j in seq_along(p_values)) {
    predictions <- numeric(nrow(data))

    for (i in seq_len(nrow(data))) {
      predictions[i] <- predict_idw(
        train = data[-i, ],
        new_locations = data[i, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE],
        p = p_values[j]
      )
    }

    stopifnot(all(is.finite(predictions)))
    cv_rmse[j] <- sqrt(mean((data$head - predictions)^2))
  }

  list(
    best_p = p_values[which.min(cv_rmse)],
    scores = data.frame(p = p_values, RMSE_m = cv_rmse)
  )
}
```

## 2B. Compare predictions at the same held-out locations

I use five balanced groups of 17 locations. For each group, I choose p using only the other 68 measurements, then predict the hidden group. This is nested cross-validation: the inner loop chooses p and the outer loop checks predictions. Each measurement is scored once in the outer loop. Random folds assess prediction among this sampling network. They do not establish performance in a distant or completely unsampled region.

```{r held-out-comparison}
set.seed(2026)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(dat)))
cv_idw <- cv_mba <- numeric(nrow(dat))
selected_p <- numeric(5)
outside_training_hull <- logical(nrow(dat))
mba_h <- 8

for (k in 1:5) {
  test_rows <- which(fold == k)
  train <- dat[-test_rows, ]
  test_xy <- dat[test_rows, c("x", "y")]

  message("Part 2: evaluating held-out group ", k, " of 5")
  tuning <- choose_idw_p(train)
  selected_p[k] <- tuning$best_p
  cv_idw[test_rows] <- predict_idw(train, test_xy, tuning$best_p)
  cv_mba[test_rows] <- MBA::mba.points(
    xyz = train[, c("x", "y", "head")], xy.est = test_xy,
    n = 1, m = 1, h = mba_h, extend = TRUE, verbose = FALSE
  )$xyz.est[, 3]

  # Some hidden sites can lie beyond the training sites' convex hull.
  # I keep them for both methods and count them, instead of dropping them.
  hull <- chull(train$x, train$y)
  outside_training_hull[test_rows] <- sp::point.in.polygon(
    test_xy$x, test_xy$y, train$x[hull], train$y[hull]
  ) == 0
}

# extend = TRUE allows MBA to include boundary test coordinates in its
# domain. It does not supply the hidden head values to the fitted surface.
stopifnot(all(is.finite(cv_idw)), all(is.finite(cv_mba)))
scores <- data.frame(
  Method = c("IDW (p chosen within training data)", "MBA (h = 8)"),
  RMSE_m = c(sqrt(mean((cv_idw - dat$head)^2)),
             sqrt(mean((cv_mba - dat$head)^2))),
  MAE_m = c(mean(abs(cv_idw - dat$head)), mean(abs(cv_mba - dat$head))),
  Mean_error_m = c(mean(cv_idw - dat$head), mean(cv_mba - dat$head))
)
fold_results <- data.frame(fold = 1:5, selected_p = selected_p)
cv_predictions <- data.frame(
  dat, fold = fold, IDW = cv_idw, MBA = cv_mba,
  outside_training_hull = outside_training_hull
)
write.csv(scores, file.path(out, "part2_prediction_scores.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(fold_results, file.path(out, "part2_power_by_fold.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(cv_predictions, file.path(out, "part2_held_out_predictions.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)
```

## 2C. Interpolate on a 20 × 20 grid

Now that the comparison is complete, I choose p again using all 85 sites. This final p is used for the map. Its tuning RMSE is not substituted for the outer cross-validation score reported above.

```{r interpolate-grid}
message("Part 2: choosing the final power for the grid")
final_tuning <- choose_idw_p(dat)
best_p <- final_tuning$best_p
write.csv(final_tuning$scores, file.path(out, "part2_idw_power_tuning.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)

grid_x <- seq(min(dat$x), max(dat$x), length.out = 20)
grid_y <- seq(min(dat$y), max(dat$y), length.out = 20)
grid <- expand.grid(x = grid_x, y = grid_y)
grid$IDW <- predict_idw(dat, grid[, c("x", "y")], best_p)

mba_surface <- MBA::mba.surf(
  xyz = dat[, c("x", "y", "head")], no.X = 20, no.Y = 20,
  n = 1, m = 1, h = mba_h, extend = TRUE
)$xyz.est

# Check that the two methods really use the same coordinates and ordering.
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(grid_x, mba_surface$x, check.attributes = FALSE)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(grid_y, mba_surface$y, check.attributes = FALSE))
)
grid$MBA <- as.vector(mba_surface$z)

# I also check mba.points against mba.surf on these same grid coordinates.
mba_grid_check <- MBA::mba.points(
  dat[, c("x", "y", "head")], grid[, c("x", "y")],
  n = 1, m = 1, h = mba_h, extend = TRUE, verbose = FALSE
)$xyz.est[, 3]
stopifnot(nrow(grid) == 400, all(is.finite(grid$IDW)),
          all(is.finite(grid$MBA)),
          max(abs(grid$MBA - mba_grid_check)) < 1e-6)

hull <- chull(dat$x, dat$y)
hull <- c(hull, hull[1])
grid$inside_hull <- sp::point.in.polygon(
  grid$x, grid$y, dat$x[hull], dat$y[hull]
) > 0
write.csv(grid, file.path(out, "part2_grid_20x20.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# The rectangle includes locations outside the observation convex hull.
# I show all 400 predictions as requested and mark the hull on the maps.
# Predictions outside it are extrapolations and deserve more caution.
```

}

points(dat$head, cv_mba, pch = 17, col = "#B2182B")

## 2E. Numerical results

```{r part2-numeric-output}
cat("\nPART 2: RESULTS\n")
print(fold_results, row.names = FALSE)
print(scores, row.names = FALSE, digits = 5)
cat("Final IDW power for the 20 x 20 map:", best_p, "\n")
cat("Minimum full-data tuning RMSE:", min(final_tuning$scores$RMSE_m), "m\n")
cat("Held-out locations outside their training hull:",
    sum(outside_training_hull), "of", nrow(dat), "\n")
cat("Grid predictions outside the observation hull:",
    sum(!grid$inside_hull), "of", nrow(grid), "\n")
capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = file.path(out, "sessionInfo.txt"))
```

## 2F. My results and discussion

These are the results from the code above, rounded to two decimal places.

For the final map, the best candidate was **p = 4**. Its leave-one-out RMSE was **65.11 m**, compared with **75.01 m** for p = 2.

| Method | RMSE (m) | MAE (m) | Mean error (m) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| IDW, p tuned in training | 65.85 | 49.47 | -15.25 |
| Multilevel B-splines | 61.57 | 47.38 | -11.50 |

The powers chosen within folds 1 to 5 were 5, 3.5, 3.5, 5 and 4. These scores use all 85 held-out predictions. I pooled their errors before calculating RMSE, rather than averaging the five fold RMSEs.

### What I learned about p

My function chose p = 4 from the candidate values. This agrees with the lowest point of the tuning curve. Small powers performed worse because distant observations received more weight. However, making p larger and larger did not keep improving the result. The curve is quite flat around its minimum: p = 3.5 gave RMSE 65.17 m, very close to 65.11 m for p = 4. I would therefore describe 4 as the best value among those I checked, not as a precisely known or universally optimal power.

### What I learned from the method comparison

B-splines gave the lower held-out RMSE: 61.57 m compared with 65.85 m for IDW. This is a reduction of about 4.29 m, or 6.5%. The MAE also favoured B-splines, although the difference was small. Both mean errors were negative, so both methods underpredicted on average in this comparison.

I kept the final-map tuning score (65.11 m) separate from IDW's comparison score (65.85 m). The first helped choose p using all the data. The second came from hidden observations that were not used to choose their p. Comparing the minimum tuning score directly with the B-spline score would give IDW an advantage from selecting its best result on those data.

### What I learned from the maps

Both methods reproduce the main pattern: higher heads in the southwest and lower heads in the northeast. Their local predictions differ, but a visually smoother surface is not automatically more accurate. I used held-out prediction errors, rather than appearance or differences between the maps, to decide which method performed better in this experiment. I also avoided judging accuracy from predictions at the fitting sites: an interpolator can reproduce those values and still predict poorly at new locations.

### Limitations and my conclusion

The 20 x 20 grid has 400 locations. Of these, 140 lie outside the convex hull of the observed sites, so those map values are extrapolations. Eleven held-out sites were also outside their training set's hull. I kept those sites in the comparison for both methods; the scores therefore include some boundary extrapolation as well as interpolation.

My folds are random, so nearby training and test sites can occur. This evaluates prediction within the existing network, not prediction across large unsampled gaps. Spatially separated folds would address that other question. A different split may also change the numerical comparison.

I used the default B-spline settings, including h = 8, without tuning h. Therefore, this compares tuned IDW with that particular B-spline setup. I have not shown that the difference is statistically significant or that either method supplies reliable prediction uncertainty.

For this experiment, I would prefer the B-spline predictions because both RMSE and MAE were lower. IDW with p = 4 remains a straightforward alternative and captures the broad spatial pattern well. The main lesson for me is to choose settings using training data and compare methods using values that were hidden from fitting and tuning.
